warmup.q: Cassandra, three copies of every row. One replica is down. You write a balance at consistency ONE and it succeeds. Then you read it at QUORUM. What comes back?
options: An error: QUORUM can't be reached with a replica down
The new balance: QUORUM has to ask both live replicas, and the one that acknowledged the write is one of them
Possibly the old balance: ONE only promised one copy
The old balance, until the down replica comes back
warmup.why: QUORUM needs 2 of 3, and with one replica down only two are alive, so the read asks both. The write was acknowledged by at least one of those two, so the read meets it. "ONE only promised one copy" is the right worry in general; here the dead node forces the overlap. The read would fail only with two replicas down.

sections.h: Copies disagree because one write can't reach every copy at the same instant
sections.html:
Lesson 1 gave every key N copies on N different nodes, so the key survives when a node dies. A copy is only useful while it's up to date, so a replicated store has to answer two questions. How does a write reach all N copies? And when a read finds copies that disagree, which one does it believe?

There are two families of answers. The first picks a leader. One copy takes every write, puts the writes in order and ships them to the others, the followers. DynamoDB works this way, as lesson 1 said. Its 2022 paper adds the detail that matters here: the leader acknowledges a write once a quorum of the partition's replicas has stored it in their logs, and only the leader serves strongly consistent reads. MongoDB's replica sets (lesson 8) and PostgreSQL's streaming replicas are leader-based too. You get one clear order of writes, and you pay with an election whenever the leader dies.

The second family has no leader, and this lesson is about it. Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak let any node take a request. That node, the coordinator, sends the write to all N replicas at once; the Cassandra docs say writes are "always sent to all replicas, regardless of consistency level". There's no election and no single node that every write waits for. But nothing puts the replicas in step either, so for a while they can disagree.

How long should the coordinator wait before it tells the client "done"? Build it up with N = 3.

Version 1 waits for all three acknowledgements, W = 3. Every read is then safe, but every write is as slow as the slowest of three machines, and with one replica down nothing can be written at all.

Version 2 waits for one, W = 1. Writes are fast and almost always possible. But a read that asks a different replica than the one that answered can miss the write.

Version 3 waits for some, and that's where N, R and W come in. W is how many replicas must confirm a write, and R is how many replicas a read asks. To decide between disagreeing answers, every value carries the timestamp of its write, and the newer one wins; Cassandra calls this rule last write wins.

A write lands on some of the N copies, a read looks at some of them, and the read is right when those two sets overlap. The rest of the lesson is about when they do.

try.title: Start three nodes and find the three copies
steps: If lesson 5's cluster isn't running, start it from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml up -d --wait (about 3 to 4 minutes, about 3 GB of Docker memory). Then load the table: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-06-balances.cql. It creates keyspace payments with three copies in datacenter dc1 and writes three balances at ALL.
Check the cluster: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool status payments. UN means up and normal.
Ask where A-1001 lives: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool getendpoints payments balances A-1001. Leave the cluster running for the next three Try-its.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra: Dynamo architecture (replication, consistency levels)

sections.h: R + W > N: why two quorums always share a copy
sections.html:
Take N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2. The write is on at least two of the three replicas, and the read asks two of the three. Two plus two is four, and there are only three replicas, so at least one replica is in both sets. That replica has the write, its timestamp is the newest the read sees, and the coordinator returns it. In general, R + W > N guarantees that every read overlaps every acknowledged write. That's the rule from lesson 1, and the reason for it fits in one sentence: you can't fit R + W different replicas into N.

The table shows the choices for N = 3:

W R R + W > 3? good for
1 1 no speed; reads may be stale
2 2 yes the common default; one replica can be down for both
1 3 yes fast writes, slow reads that need every replica
3 1 yes fast reads; any one dead replica blocks writes

Dynamo's paper calls (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2) the common configuration among Amazon's services. It also describes read-heavy services that set R = 1 and W = N.

R and W also decide what you can do while nodes are down. A write needs W replicas up and a read needs R. With one of three down, R = 2 and W = 2 both still work. With two down, both fail, and the coordinator refuses before it even tries.

Cassandra lets each request choose, with consistency levels: ONE, TWO, QUORUM (a majority, n/2 + 1, so 2 of 3), ALL, LOCAL_QUORUM (a majority in the coordinator's datacenter) and ANY (for writes; a stored hint counts). cqlsh starts at ONE, and the Java driver 4.19 defaults to LOCAL_ONE, so you're at R = 1 and W = 1 until you choose otherwise. Writing and reading at QUORUM gives 2 + 2 > 3.

The stepper runs one write at W = 1 with a replica down, then reads at R = 1 and R = 2. Watch the fifth frame closely. The R = 2 read is right there only because the write happened to reach two replicas, not because W promised it, and the last frame shows the run where it doesn't.

stepper.title: One write at W = 1, then reads at R = 1 and R = 2
stepper.intro: N = 3 replicas of A-1001's balance. Values carry the timestamp of their write.

refs.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, sections 4.5 and 6 (SOSP 2007, PDF)

sections.h: Three ways a stale copy catches up: hints, read repair and anti-entropy
sections.html:
A replica that missed writes has to catch up somehow, or it stays wrong forever. Leaderless stores use three mechanisms, each for a different case.

Hinted handoff covers a replica that's down for a short time. When a replica doesn't answer, the coordinator keeps the write for it as a hint and sends it over when the replica comes back. In Dynamo the hint goes to a stand-in node, as lesson 1's stepper showed; Cassandra keeps it on the coordinator itself, in files named after the down node's host ID. The cassandra.yaml in 5.0.9 sets max_hint_window: 3h. A node that stays down longer stops getting hints and needs one of the other two mechanisms. The docs call hints best-effort, and that's accurate: a coordinator that is lost for good takes its unsent hints with it.

Read repair happens on the read path. When a read asks R replicas and their answers differ, the coordinator writes the newest version back to the stale ones it asked, as in the stepper's sixth frame. Cassandra does it cheaply. One replica returns the data and the others return only a digest, a hash of their answer. If the digests match, the read is done. If they don't, the coordinator fetches full data, picks the newest and sends a repair. At QUORUM it waits for that repair before it answers, so afterwards a majority holds the new value, and any later quorum read overlaps it. Read repair only fixes keys that somebody reads, on replicas that the read asked.

Anti-entropy covers the rest: rows nobody reads, and nodes that were down past the hint window. Two replicas compare everything they hold for a range of tokens. Sending every row to compare would be far too much traffic, so each replica builds a Merkle tree. The leaves are hashes of individual keys and every parent is the hash of its children, so equal roots mean equal ranges. When roots differ, the replicas compare the children and walk down only the branches that differ, until they reach the keys that are out of sync (Dynamo, section 4.7). The figure shows one such walk. In Cassandra this is nodetool repair, which operators run on a schedule. Lesson 7 shows why that schedule has a deadline: a delete is a tombstone, and a node that misses one for longer than gc_grace_seconds can bring the deleted data back.

sections.h: Where R + W > N stops protecting you
sections.html:
R + W > N makes the read and write sets overlap. It doesn't make a leaderless store behave like one machine, and four cases show the gap.

The first is the sloppy quorum. Dynamo writes to the first N healthy nodes, so when a home replica is down a stand-in takes the write and counts toward W. A later read of the home replicas can miss the stand-in completely, R + W > N or not. Cassandra doesn't count hints toward any level above ANY, which is one reason a Cassandra write can be refused where a Dynamo write wasn't.

The second is that a failed write isn't undone. If the coordinator gets fewer than W acknowledgements in time, the client sees an error, but the replicas that stored the write keep it, and later reads may return it. The Try-it below makes one: a write at ALL fails with WriteTimeout, and the next read returns the "failed" value. Treat a timeout as "unknown", and make retries idempotent the way lesson 3 did.

The third is concurrent writes. Two clients write the same balance at nearly the same moment. Both writes succeed, and the replicas keep the one with the higher timestamp. The other one is gone without an error. Timestamps come from clocks, and clocks drift. Lesson 9 is about this, and about vector clocks, Dynamo's answer.

The fourth is reads during a write. While a write is still reaching replicas, one quorum read can meet it and a quorum read a moment later can miss it, unless read repair blocks as Cassandra's does at QUORUM. Abadi's PACELC paper puts it plainly: "simply using a quorum protocol is not sufficient" for the strongest consistency, linearizability, where the store behaves as if there were one copy and every read sees the latest completed write. Lesson 9 defines it properly. Lesson 10 covers what Cassandra offers when you need a real compare-and-set: lightweight transactions, which run Paxos.

So what should you use? For a balance that drives decisions, read and write at QUORUM (LOCAL_QUORUM with several datacenters), keep writes idempotent, and use a lightweight transaction where two writers race on one row. For data where a stale read costs nothing, such as a merchant's daily view rebuilt from Kafka, ONE is fine, and it keeps working with two of the three replicas down.

Two questions this lesson leaves open are how a node learns that another is down, and how a Cassandra cluster is wired together at all. Lesson 13 answers both: the token ring with virtual nodes, the gossip protocol, and the failure detector. Lesson 14 then sets up and runs a real cluster.

The coordinator thought cass3 was alive, so it tried, waited write_request_timeout (2 seconds in this cassandra.yaml) for the third answer, and reported failure. Two replicas had already stored 3000, nothing undid it, and the next read at ONE returned it. Compare with the last Try-it: Unavailable means "not attempted", WriteTimeout means "attempted, outcome unknown". Your code has to treat the second as possibly applied.

refs.title: Abadi, Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (IEEE Computer 2012, PDF)

analogy: Think of three clerks who each keep a copy of the same ledger page. A new entry is phoned to all three. W is how many clerks must say "written" before you hang up; R is how many you call when you want to read the page, keeping the entry with the latest time stamp. Call two to write and two to read, and some clerk is always in both calls. A clerk who was out to lunch finds a note on the desk when they're back (a hint). If you call two clerks and they disagree, you tell the one who's behind (read repair). Once a week they compare page summaries and fix whatever differs (anti-entropy). The analogy breaks on time: real clerks would notice two entries made at the same moment, while the store keeps the one with the later clock reading and quietly drops the other, and its clocks can be wrong.
world: Your Oracle primary with a Data Guard standby is the leader-based family: one place takes writes, in one order. Cassandra hands you the dial instead, per statement, and the Java driver starts at LOCAL_ONE. For a balance or a payment status that a Quarkus service reads to make a decision, set LOCAL_QUORUM on both the write and the read, in the driver's configuration rather than statement by statement, so nobody forgets. For a merchant's daily view that a Kafka consumer rebuilds anyway, LOCAL_ONE is fine. And treat a WriteTimeoutException like an HTTP timeout to the card issuer: the write may have landed. A Temporal activity that retries it must write the same value with the same key, so a second attempt changes nothing.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading "we write at QUORUM" as "our writes are atomic and our reads are current". People see 2 + 2 > 3 and stop thinking. Then a write times out, the service reports failure to the client, and the balance changes anyway, because two replicas had stored it. Or two services update the same row at once and one update silently disappears, because the replicas keep the later timestamp. The fix is to treat quorums as what they are, an overlap guarantee for acknowledged writes. Make every write idempotent, treat a timeout as unknown rather than failed, and use a lightweight transaction (lesson 10) where two writers can race on one row.

compare.title: Choosing R and W: Cassandra per request, DynamoDB per partition

a.label: Cassandra (leaderless)
a.title: cqlsh
a.html: -- every statement picks its own W or R CONSISTENCY ONE; -- W = 1: fast, works with 2 of 3 replicas down UPDATE payments.balances SET balance_minor = 7000 WHERE account_id = 'A-1001'; CONSISTENCY QUORUM; -- R = 2: overlaps any QUORUM write (2 + 2 > 3) SELECT balance_minor FROM payments.balances WHERE account_id = 'A-1001';

b.label: DynamoDB (a leader per partition)
b.title: AWS SDK for Java 2.x
b.html: // every write goes to the partition's leader, which answers once // a quorum of the partition's replicas has logged it ddb.putItem { it.tableName("payments").item(profile) } // a read picks: any replica, half price, may be behind ... ddb.getItem { it.tableName("payments").key(key) } // ... or the leader, which has every acknowledged write ddb.getItem { it.tableName("payments").key(key).consistentRead(true) }

compare.note: Cassandra exposes the quorum arithmetic, and each statement chooses its R or W. That's flexible, and it's also easy to get wrong statement by statement. DynamoDB fixes the write side for you: the leader orders writes and waits for a quorum of replicas, so you only choose how to read. An eventually consistent read can come from any replica and may miss a recent write; a strongly consistent read goes to the leader. Neither design lets two concurrent writers both win: Cassandra keeps the later timestamp, and DynamoDB applies them in the leader's order.

worked.title: Choose N, R and W for two payment tables

steps.say: Write down what each table must survive and what a stale read costs. Balances drive authorization decisions; the merchant daily view is rebuilt from a Kafka topic every few minutes.
steps.code:
table               a stale read means               must keep working with
balances            approving a payment twice        one replica down

2 + 2 = 4 > 3        -> every read overlaps every acknowledged write

lab.title: Build a quorum simulator with failures and read repair
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All nine fail with NotImplementedError.

Read QuorumStore.kt. The replicas, fail, recover, valueAt, the private storeIfNewer and subsets are given. Every write and read names its own W or R, as a Cassandra statement names its consistency level.

Write write: refuse with Unavailable when fewer than w replicas are up, stamp the next clock tick, store on every up replica in reaches, and count the acknowledgements. Three tests pass, including the one where a timed-out write stays on the replica it reached.
Write read: ask the first r up replicas in order, keep the newest timestamp, and repair the stale replicas you asked. Five more pass.

Write staleReadPossible by brute force with subsets. The test checks your answer against R + W > N for every N up to 5. The last test runs 2,000 random steps of failures and lost messages at W = 2, R = 2. Change its w = 2 to w = 1, watch it fail at some step, and put it back.
hints: replicas.count { it.up } is how many replicas the coordinator believes are alive. Check it before you touch clock.
order.map(::replica).filter { it.up }.take(r) is the set of replicas a read asks.
maxByOrNull { it.timestamp } picks the newest version. A replica with no version for the key counts as older than any version.
Repair with the given storeIfNewer, so a repair can never overwrite something newer.
In staleReadPossible, two sets miss each other when readSet.none { it in writeSet }. One such pair is enough to return true.

answer.html:
W  R   read sees last acked write?   down, writes work   down, reads work
1  1   no  (1 + 1 = 2)               2                   2
2  2   yes (2 + 2 = 4)               1                   1
1  3   yes (1 + 3 = 4)               2                   0
3  1   yes (3 + 1 = 4)               0                   2

Why: a write set of W replicas and a read set of R replicas can't both fit
into N replicas without sharing one when R + W > N, and the shared replica
has the write, with the newest timestamp the read sees.

recap: Leader-based stores (DynamoDB, MongoDB) order writes at one copy; leaderless stores (Dynamo, Cassandra) send every write to all N replicas and wait for W acknowledgements, and a read asks R replicas and keeps the newest timestamp.
R + W > N makes every read set overlap every acknowledged write set. For N = 3, QUORUM is 2, and QUORUM writes plus QUORUM reads survive one replica down.
Cassandra chooses W or R per statement with consistency levels. cqlsh starts at ONE and the Java driver 4.19 at LOCAL_ONE, so you start at R = W = 1.
Stale copies catch up three ways: hinted handoff for short outages (3 hours by default), read repair on keys that get read, and anti-entropy repair with Merkle trees for everything else.

Quorums aren't transactions: a timed-out write may have landed, concurrent writes lose to the later timestamp, and quorum reads aren't linearizable. Make writes idempotent and use lightweight transactions for races.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "We write and read balances at QUORUM, so Cassandra is strongly consistent for us, like Oracle." Explain what that setting does guarantee and what it doesn't.
explain.answer: With three replicas, QUORUM means two. A write is acknowledged once two replicas have it, and a read asks two replicas and keeps the newest timestamp. Two plus two is more than three, so every read set shares a replica with every acknowledged write set, and the read sees that write. That's the guarantee, and it survives one replica being down. It isn't Oracle, though. If a write times out, the client sees an error but the replicas that stored it keep it, so the balance may have changed. If two services write the same balance at the same time, both succeed and the replicas keep whichever has the later timestamp, so one update silently disappears. Quorum reads also aren't linearizable in general, though Cassandra's blocking read repair at QUORUM keeps a later quorum read from going backwards. So we keep writes idempotent, treat timeouts as unknown, and use a lightweight transaction where two writers can race on one row.

deeper.html:
How does a node know another is down? Dynamo's section 4.8 describes a gossip protocol: every second, each node contacts a peer chosen at random, and the two reconcile what they know about membership. Failure detection is purely local in Dynamo: node A treats B as failed if B doesn't answer A's messages, whatever B looks like to others. Cassandra does the same with gossip, and every node runs a variant of the Phi Accrual failure detector, which turns the gaps between heartbeats into a suspicion level rather than a yes-or-no timeout. That's why docker compose pause fooled the coordinator in the last Try-it for a few seconds: a frozen process looks alive until enough heartbeats are missing.

Anti-entropy in practice, from the same cluster (output trimmed). With hints switched off, cass3 missed a write to A-2002 while it was stopped, and a full repair of the keyspace fixed it:

$ nodetool repair --full payments
[2026-11-07 19:03:07,566] Starting repair command #1 (...), repairing keyspace payments with repair options (parallelism: parallel, primary range: false, incremental: false, ...)
[2026-11-07 19:03:07,998] Repair completed successfully
[2026-11-07 19:03:08,000] Repair command #1 finished in 0 seconds

After it, a read at ONE on cass3 returned the new balance. Real clusters run incremental repair, which only compares data written since the last repair, and schedule it with a tool, because a full repair of terabytes takes hours and every node takes part.

The Dynamo paper also has a small trick for read-your-writes. A write usually follows a read, so the coordinator for the write is chosen as the node that answered the preceding read fastest. That node then has the new version, and the client's next read is likely to reach it. It raises the chance of reading your own write without promising it.
